question: Cambridge, 1967. A radio telescope picks up a pulse every 1.337 seconds, regular as a clock. What is sending it?
answer: A dead star: a neutron star, the city-sized core left by a supernova, spinning and sweeping a radio beam past Earth like a lighthouse. Jocelyn Bell, a PhD student, first spotted it as a smudge on chart paper. Thousands of pulsars are now known, each a beacon nobody built.
move: Ask what the exciting explanation would also have to show, then look for it.
ask: Which exciting explanation do I believe without checking what else it would have to show?

clues.text: Pulses every 1.337 seconds, so steady it is nicknamed LGM-1: little green men.
It returns 4 minutes earlier each day: it keeps time with the stars, not the Sun.
Low radio pitches arrive after high ones: the pulses crossed light-years of gas.
No Doppler wobble: the sender is not circling a star, as a planet would.
A second source turns up elsewhere in the sky, with its own beat.

scene.why: A world with senders on it would swing round its sun, and its signal with it. This one didn't move.

reference: Hewish, Bell, Pilkington, Scott & Collins, Observation of a rapidly pulsating radio source, Nature 217:709-713, 1968, doi:10.1038/217709a0
